=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s position

The Seller’s package materially favours Harbourglass. It combines a broad disclosure and buyer-knowledge exclusion with limitations intended to apply to virtually every claim, while leaving significant completion risks unresolved.

**Do not accept the “reviewer efficiency note”.** The Seller’s “[STANDARD]” labels and statements that terms have been agreed are not evidence of Buyer approval. All provisions require review against the agreed deal: **100% acquisition, AUD 24 million, debt-free/cash-free, NSW law.**

This review is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter—not the underlying DD documents or complete SPA. The disclosures identify unresolved risks; they do not establish every breach or liability.

## 1. Liability and recovery protections

| Issue | Why it departs from Buyer’s interests | Recommended pushback |
|---|---|---|
| **General warranty cap: AUD 4.8m** | A 20% cap may leave substantial losses unrecovered. Its adequacy depends on diligence, warranty coverage and the other exclusions—not whether it is labelled “standard”. | Seek a higher general cap. At minimum, assess it separately from fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities and other contractual obligations. Confirm Seller creditworthiness and consider escrow, retention or other security. |
| **AUD 25,000 de minimis; AUD 250,000 deductible basket** | Small claims disappear, and Buyer permanently bears the first AUD 250,000 of otherwise qualifying claims. Separate claims from the same underlying problem could fall below the threshold. | Reduce thresholds; seek a tipping basket, under which qualifying losses become recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded. Aggregate related claims. Exclude fundamental claims, tax, specific indemnities and price adjustments from these thresholds. |
| **18-month general warranty period** | Problems may emerge only through later audits, renewals or regulatory enquiries. More seriously, the proposed default would extend this short limit to all claims. | Seek at least 24 months for general warranties, with separately negotiated periods for other categories. Ensure timely notified claims survive resolution and notice requirements do not defeat otherwise valid claims through technicalities. |
| **Capacity and title subject to general limits** | Buyer could pay AUD 24m but recover only AUD 4.8m if Seller cannot transfer the agreed shares. “Administrative simplicity” is no justification. | Separate fundamental warranties covering capacity, authority, ownership, fully paid shares and freedom from encumbrances. Seek a purchase-price-level cap and a substantially longer claim period appropriate to the execution form and applicable limitation rules. |
| **Tax and IP treated as settled under the general regime** | Neither should be treated as settled without Buyer agreement. Historic tax liabilities may emerge well after 18 months; deficient IP ownership could undermine the acquired business. | Obtain a standalone pre-Completion tax indemnity with appropriate exceptions and a period aligned to relevant assessment/review periods, commonly negotiated around seven years. Negotiate IP coverage, cap and survival separately, supported by the specific Ironquay protections below. |
| **Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to all claims** | This could cap or exclude claims for failure to repay debt, deliver releases, comply with covenants, pay adjustments or satisfy indemnities—not just inaccurate warranties. | Replace “all Claims” treatment with an express claim-category matrix. Preserve enforcement, debt/payment claims, adjustment rights and appropriate equitable relief. Carve out fraud, fraudulent concealment and liabilities that cannot lawfully be excluded; scrutinise any attempt to defeat misleading-conduct claims. Do not assume an overbroad clause will simply be unenforceable. |

**Read clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 together.** A valuable indemnity is not useful if another clause subjects it to the general cap, basket, short time bar or disclosure defence.

## 2. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge

### Blanket data-room and public-register disclosure

General disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room potentially transfers the burden of finding and understanding risks to Buyer. References may also incorporate material Buyer never actually received.

Push for:

- A **fair-disclosure standard** requiring enough detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter.
- Specific, intelligible disclosure against relevant warranties, rather than indiscriminate document dumping.
- A frozen, indexed and retained data-room copy, with a controlled process for later disclosures.
- Narrowly identified public-register searches, documents and dates—not all theoretically searchable material.
- No disclosure qualification of fundamental warranties, specific indemnities or express completion obligations unless specifically agreed.

Disclosure may qualify warranties; **it should not be treated as Buyer acceptance of the risk or waiver of a required remedy.**

### Constructive knowledge exclusion

Clause 8.3 extends beyond actual knowledge to whatever Buyer or its advisers could have discovered. That could substantially hollow out warranty protection.

**Primary position: delete it.** If unavoidable, limit it to actual conscious knowledge of named Buyer deal-team members, without imputed adviser knowledge or a duty to investigate. Preserve agreed specific indemnities and completion protections despite Buyer knowledge.

## 3. Material transaction-specific issues

### A. Bluefen — critical completion condition

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. No final consent or evidence satisfying its associated conditions has been supplied.

Delivery of a written consent alone is insufficient if clause 11.3 conditions remain outstanding, the consent is conditional or revocable, or it introduces adverse commercial terms.

**Pushback:**
- Completion conditional on a valid, effective consent and satisfaction of all associated conditions.
- No materially adverse amendments, fees or concessions without Buyer approval.
- Buyer-controlled waiver, an appropriate long-stop date and termination rights if unresolved.
- Evidence sufficient to verify compliance—not merely Seller’s “reasonable endeavours”.

### B. Riverlark — discharge at Completion, not afterwards

Approximately **AUD 3.2m** remains outstanding. A promise to release security after Completion leaves Buyer owning a company with outstanding debt/security and potential change-control consequences.

Require a lender payoff statement, settlement arrangements and effective release of security and relevant guarantees **at Completion**, with filing evidence or appropriate binding release undertakings where registration follows later.

The funds flow must reconcile the debt repayment with the AUD 24m debt-free/cash-free price. **Do not pay Seller the full equity proceeds and leave Buyer to fund historic debt separately; equally, avoid deducting the same debt twice.**

### C. Ironquay — ownership, not just an unpaid invoice

The disclosed contractual condition suggests transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The AUD 180,000 open balance is a warning sign, but is not conclusive evidence of non-payment.

An indemnity limited to that payment does not address losses from missing IP rights, infringement allegations or interruption to exploitation of the materials.

Require:
- Verification of the complete payment position and satisfaction of transfer conditions.
- Payment by Seller or through an agreed Seller-funded completion mechanism.
- Confirmation of ownership transfer and an effective confirmatory assignment where needed, including necessary rights to embedded third-party materials.
- A broader specific indemnity for losses arising from the pre-Completion ownership/payment defect, outside the general warranty limitations.

If the materials are business-critical, remediation should be a completion requirement, not merely a damages remedy.

### D. Completion bonuses — omitted economic liability

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional, not necessarily presently payable. Nevertheless, Completion may trigger a material target-company liability. Calling them “a matter for Seller” does not allocate that liability or fund it.

Verify the employment and payment conditions, who owes the amounts, and applicable payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs. Require an express Seller-funded treatment through the price mechanism, funds flow or specific indemnity. Prevent double counting with debt, working capital or other adjustments.

### E. Export/privacy incident — investigate before concluding

The record identifies an unintended external download link involving potentially **1,240 records**. It does **not** establish unauthorised access, a notifiable breach or a quantified loss. Equally, Seller has no sound basis to dismiss it as immaterial while investigation remains preliminary.

Require prompt evidence preservation, containment and investigation into access, scope and affected data; assess applicable privacy and contractual notification duties. Preserve timely legally required notifications.

Seek a specific indemnity for pre-Completion incident liabilities, investigation, remediation and third-party claims, with appropriate control/cooperation provisions and separate survival. Buyer should retain control of post-Completion systems and regulatory compliance.

### F. Supplier renewals — assess the AUD 330,000 aggregate

Three related AUD 110,000 renewals should be reviewed together. “Ordinary course” is an unsupported conclusion, not established by the disclosure.

Check timing, scope, termination rights, accruals, commercial necessity and whether commitments were accelerated or entered into outside agreed pre-Completion controls. Apply aggregate consent thresholds to related commitments to prevent splitting.

Normal future operating expenditure is not automatically Seller debt. But unusual or value-reducing commitments may justify consent rights, a price adjustment or specific protection.

### G. Lease and Mossvale — do not invent consent requirements

The supplied descriptions distinguish:
- **Office lease:** a notification obligation.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction, not an express share-sale consent requirement.

Review the full clauses, comply with genuine notice obligations and check for separate change-control provisions. Do not demand unnecessary consents on the assumption that a share sale is an assignment.

### H. Share title — register is evidence, not complete verification

DD-012 records Seller as holder of all issued shares. That is useful evidence, but does not independently resolve beneficial ownership, encumbrances, options, competing rights or transfer restrictions.

Verify the capital structure, constitution, relevant shareholder arrangements, issue/transfer records and applicable searches. Require fundamental warranties and completion deliverables transferring **100% of the fully paid shares free of encumbrances**, with releases and corporate approvals as necessary.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Completion gates:** effective Bluefen consent and conditions; Riverlark repayment/release; verified share title; remediation of business-critical Ironquay ownership issues.
2. **Economic protection:** reconcile the AUD 24m price and funds flow, including debt, bonuses/on-costs and any outstanding Ironquay payment, without double counting.
3. **Meaningful recourse:** reject universal limitations; negotiate separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes and adequate recovery security.
4. **Preserve warranties:** narrow disclosure and remove constructive/imputed Buyer knowledge exclusions.
5. **Close factual gaps:** investigate the export incident and related supplier renewals before accepting Seller’s materiality and ordinary-course conclusions.

**Bottom line:** disclosure of an unresolved issue is not a solution. Known risks need an express allocation through completion conditions, remediation, price treatment or a properly protected specific indemnity—not reliance on general warranties that the Seller’s own drafting may neutralise.
